title: Counting Important Terms · Level 1
slo: Explain how frequency analysis and TF-IDF identify document topics.

exercises.question_text: Which facts describe Inverse Document Frequency (IDF)? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: IDF checks whether a term is common or rare across a collection. Rarer terms have more distinguishing value.

options.text: It uses total document count N
options.rationale: N is the total number of items in the IDF formula. It is divided by df(t).

options.text: A term in every document has IDF zero
options.rationale: When df(t) equals N, the ratio is 1. The logarithm of 1 is zero.

options.text: It counts uses in one document
options.rationale: Counting uses in one item is TF. IDF depends on how many items contain the term.

feedback.intrinsic: You would mistake a collection measure for a local count.
feedback.instructional: IDF uses N and df(t); TF counts appearances in one item.

exercises.explanation: Correct. IDF reflects how widely a term occurs across a collection.

options.rationale: TF-IDF multiplies TF by IDF. It combines occurrence in one item with rarity across the collection.
TF-IDF is based on term counts and collection rarity. It does not use grammar or word order.

feedback.intrinsic: You would look for language structure instead of distinctive terms.
feedback.instructional: TF-IDF combines a within-item count with collection-wide rarity.

options.rationale: Nodes and edges are part of TextRank. TF-IDF is calculated from TF and IDF.
options.better_fit: Choose this when describing TextRank’s graph.

feedback.intrinsic: You would use a graph idea instead of a relevance score.
feedback.instructional: TF-IDF does not rank graph nodes; it multiplies TF and IDF.

options.rationale: Vectors and cosine similarity are semantic-model methods. TF-IDF uses frequencies and inverse document frequency.
options.better_fit: Choose this when comparing semantic similarity between vectors.

feedback.intrinsic: You would compare vector meanings instead of term relevance.
feedback.instructional: TF-IDF is a statistical score based on TF and IDF.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TF-IDF combines how often a term appears with how rare it is across the collection.

exercises.question_text: If a term appears in every document, its IDF is zero.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A term shared everywhere would be treated as distinctive.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: If a term appears in every item, N/df(t) is 1, and log(1) is zero.

exercises.explanation: Correct. When df(t) equals N, log(N/N) equals zero.

exercises.question_text: A high TF-IDF score means a term is common in many documents.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A widely shared term would be mistaken for a strong topic clue.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A term common in many items has low IDF. High TF-IDF needs high TF and relative rarity across the collection.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A high score requires frequent use in one item and relative rarity elsewhere.

options.rationale: TF is the number of times a term appears in one item. Six appearances give a TF of 6.
Collection-wide rarity is IDF. TF is only the within-item count.

feedback.intrinsic: You would confuse a local count with collection-wide rarity.
feedback.instructional: TF counts appearances in one item; IDF checks how widely the term appears.

options.rationale: TF-IDF is the combined score. TF is one input to that calculation.
options.better_fit: Choose this when TF is multiplied by IDF.

feedback.intrinsic: You would skip the distinction between a count and a combined score.
feedback.instructional: TF is the count; TF-IDF combines that count with IDF.

options.rationale: Sentence connection scores belong to TextRank. TF counts term appearances.
options.better_fit: Choose this when ranking connected sentences for a summary.

feedback.intrinsic: You would analyze sentence links instead of term occurrences.
feedback.instructional: TF is a simple term count in one item.

exercises.explanation: Correct. TF is simply the number of appearances in one item.

exercises.question_text: Which terms may be frequent in both AI-agent documents and show only their shared theme? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: This term appears frequently in both samples. It shows their shared theme rather than a specific difference.
Both samples contain this term. It therefore has little power to separate them.
This term is common to both samples. It identifies a shared theme, not a unique topic.

options.error_type: Confuses a document-specific term with a shared term
options.rationale: Declarative is associated with the Copilot Studio sample. It helps distinguish that specific topic.
options.better_fit: Choose this when identifying the Copilot Studio sample’s specific focus.

feedback.intrinsic: You would overlook a term that separates the two article topics.
feedback.instructional: Shared terms occur in both items; document-specific terms are more useful for distinguishing them.

exercises.explanation: Correct. These shared terms do not separate the specific topics.

exercises.question_text: If a term appears six times in a document, its IDF is 6.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: A within-item count would be assigned to the wrong measure.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: TF counts appearances in one item. IDF measures rarity across the collection.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Six appearances give TF of 6, not IDF.

options.rationale: Frequency analysis counts how often each normalized token occurs. Those counts can suggest the main subject.
Rarity across a collection is measured by IDF. Frequency analysis is a count within one item.
options.better_fit: Choose this when comparing how widely a term appears across a collection.

feedback.intrinsic: You would focus on shared rarity instead of the main terms in the report.
feedback.instructional: Use frequency analysis for token counts; use IDF for collection-wide rarity.

options.rationale: Sentence links and similarity are used by TextRank. Frequency analysis does not build a graph.
options.better_fit: Choose this for extractive summaries based on connected sentences.

feedback.intrinsic: You would be summarizing sentence connections rather than counting key terms.
feedback.instructional: Frequency analysis counts normalized tokens; TextRank ranks connected sentences.

options.rationale: Vector orientation belongs to semantic embeddings. Frequency analysis uses counts rather than vectors.
options.better_fit: Choose this when comparing semantic similarity between words.

feedback.intrinsic: You would compare meanings when a simple count is needed.
feedback.instructional: Frequency analysis uses occurrences, while embeddings represent semantic relationships.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Counting normalized token occurrences can reveal the main subject.

exercises.question_text: A term common in many documents is less useful for distinguishing one document from another.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The comparison would treat a shared term as if it were distinctive.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: A term found in many items may show a general theme, but it does not identify one specific topic.

exercises.explanation: Correct. A widely shared term has little power to separate individual items.

exercises.question_text: A score calculated as TF multiplied by IDF is called ___.

parts.text: A score calculated as TF multiplied by IDF is called

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The result would be named as only part of the calculation.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: TF-IDF is the combined score from TF multiplied by IDF; TF and IDF alone are not the final score.

exercises.explanation: The score joins a term’s count in one item with its collection-wide rarity. TF and IDF are the separate inputs, while frequency analysis is simple counting.

exercises.question_text: Arrange the following steps to calculate IDF.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The calculation would no longer follow the IDF formula.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Find N and df(t) first, divide N by df(t), then take the logarithm.

exercises.correct_answer: Count all documents Find documents containing t Divide N by df(t) Take the logarithm
exercises.explanation: IDF needs both collection counts before forming N/df(t). The logarithm is applied after the ratio is calculated.

exercises.question_text: Frequency analysis finds a term's rarity across a whole collection of documents.

feedback_for_incorrect.intrinsic: The count would be used for the wrong purpose.
feedback_for_incorrect.instructional: Frequency analysis counts terms in one item. IDF measures whether a term is common or rare across a collection.

exercises.explanation: Correct. Frequency analysis counts occurrences; IDF handles collection-wide rarity.

flashcards.back: It counts normalized token occurrences to suggest a document's topic.
Shared terms cannot distinguish one document from another.
It is the number of times a term appears in one document.
It measures how rare or common a term is across documents.
